Political.
From the (N.Y.) COMMERCIAL ADVERTISER.
NUMBER VII.
To the PRESIDENT of the UNITED STATES.
SIR,

THE second observation I have to make on the principles avowed in your answer, is, that the charge alleged against your predecessor, of excluding from all office those who were not of a particular sect, is not well founded.

It will be recollected that Gen. Washington, begun his administration upon the most conciliatory principles. In distributing the offices among parties, as far as they then existed, he held a most impartial hand.

When you resigned, your place was filled by Mr. Randolph, a man of the same sect. What was the consequence? Let the answer be found in the "precious confessions" which betray the secrets of government to a foreign and insidious minister...
The history of Gen. Lamb, Collector of the port of New-York, another of the same political sect with yourself, who also was found delinquent to the amount of fifty thousand dollars or more...
Another officer of the revenue in Boston, by the name of Jarvis, of the same republican sect, was guilty of a similar breach of trust...
Mr. Monroe, minister to France, another of this favorite sect, who violated his instructions, adds another example to the list of faithless public servants.

If, after all these instances of breach of confidence in the sect, which boasted of its exclusive title to republicanism, Gen. Washington, and Mr. Adams, began to question the safety of appointing pretended republicans to office, can any sober citizen blame their doubts?

But the assertion, that "by the steady pursuits of measures [exclusion] nearly all the offices were monopolized by one sect," requires great modifications to be entitled to the character of correctness.

But Gen. Washington came into office by a unanimous vote of both parties; and the political events which gave a new character and direction to opposition, took place in 1793, and the subsequent years.

mate, their numbers, respectability & weight of character. But observe, that when offices were well filled, they have been considered as permanently filled; the former Presidents never having displaced men without substantial objections to their conduct in office.

The case is precisely similar to that of a town or city incorporated, in which, at the first choice of officers, all the free citizens should agree in the choice. But in a few months one half of them, growing discontented, form a party against the officers and their adherents and exclaim most bitterly against them for a "monopoly of offices."
EXTRACTS
From "A Dissertation on the Constitutional Freedom of the Press in the United States," a pamphlet just published by Mr. Naurice, in Boston.

"THE conduct and tenor of executive and judicial appointments ought to be the subject of scrutiny. Where the appointments are bestowed upon persons of a particular way of thinking, or on the leaders of a party, we have a just right to discover from this, the drift of the administration, and as clear a privilege openly to promulge the truth, as to the facts of appointment, and to give out our opinion of the tendency of the measures.

"It has been said that the president cannot administer the government on his own principles and plans, unless his agents and servants shall coincide with him in opinions upon civil and political subjects. This assertion, in the latitude it is intended, cannot be true, or be consistent with political propriety.

NOTICE is hereby given, that the subscriber has been duly appointed Assignee of the Estate and Effects of Zephaniah Harlow, Jun. and Freeman Harlow, of Bath, in the District of Maine. Bankrupts:—All persons having in their possession any property belonging to the said Harlows, are called upon to surrender the same; and those indebted, to make immediate payment to ANDREW GREENWOOD.

NOTIFICATION. With the subscribers, Commissioners appointed by the Hon. Edward Cuts, Esq. Judge of the Probate of Wills, &c. for the county of York, to receive and examine the claims of the several Creditors to the estate of SAMUEL ROSE, late of Biddleford, mariner deceased, represented intestate—hereby give notice, that six months from the 26th of October, 1801 is allowed to bring in and prove their claims—that we shall attend that service at the house of JOSEPH STEVENS, Administrator on said estate, in Biddleford, on the second Thursday of November instant, and the second Thursday of the four next following months, from one to five o'clock, P.M. on each day.

STRAYED from the subscriber, about the 7th inst. a dark red COW, about 5 or 6 years old, with large picked horns, and a very long tail. Whoever will give information of said Cow, so that the owner may get her again, shall be handsomely rewarded for her trouble. JACOB ROLFE.

UNAWAY from the subscriber, on Sunday last, an indentured apprentice named SAMUEL RICHARDSON, aged about 18 years. Had on when he went away, a green coat and blue trowsers—he is about five feet four inches high. Whoever will apprehend said boy, and bring him to the subscriber, shall receive one dollar reward, and no charges paid. And I do hereby forbid all persons harboring or trusting him, and all masters of vessels from shipping or receiving him on board their vessels, as they would avoid the penalty of the law. JOHN BURBANK.

FIVE CENTS REWARD. RANAWAY from the subscriber, an indentured apprentice by the name of BENJAMIN RICH, about nineteen years old—had on when he went away, a short brown jacket, & blue trowsers—brown hair. Any person who will bring back said runaway, shall receive the above reward, but no charges paid. I therefore forbid all persons harboring or trusting him, or any masters of vessels carrying him away, as they would avoid the penalty of the law. JACOB KNIGHT.

TEN CENTS REWARD. RANAWAY from the subscriber, an indentured apprentice by the name of Samuel Williams, about fifteen years old—about four feet ten inches high, short brown hair, dark hair, had on a blue coat, striped waistcoat, and grey trowsers—I hereby forbid all persons harboring him, or any masters of vessels carrying him away. Any person who will bring back said runaway, shall receive the above reward of OBED BURNHAM, of Topsham, in the county of Lincoln. October 23, 1801.

TWENTY DOLLARS REWARD. LOST from the Tenter Hooks of me the subscriber some time about the last of October, or the first of November; one piece of FULLED WOOLLEN CLOTH, of a brown color, containing about ten yards. Also from my Fulling Mill, sundry pieces of Felled Cloth, neither sheared nor pressed. Any person giving information of the same, shall on conviction be entitled to the above reward. Merchants and shopkeepers are requested to stop any such goods, should they be presented for sale. PETER MERRILL, JUN.

STOP THEIR. STOLEN from the Barn of the subscriber, in Freeport on Wednesday night the 4th instant, a large Bay HORSE, marked as follows:—A white streak in his forehead, both hind feet white, black mane and tail, carries his head very high, his nose out; When shod, had a shoe on his withers, and one or two on each hind leg; a harness crease horse, traces &c. Whoever will apprehend said Thief or Thieves and bring said Horse, and return him to the owner, shall receive the above reward and all charges paid by me, SAMUEL JAMIESON.

TWENTY DOLLARS REWARD. WHEREAS SALLY, daughter of me the subscriber, has behaved very unbecoming, and has left her home—she is therefore to forbid all persons harboring or trusting her on my account, as I will pay no account or be contracting after this date. MOSES CROSS.
